title: The Peasant's Nephew: Law, the Great Church, and the Empire Taken Back
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Dardanian Village and the Uncle's Ladder

stops.name: Tauresium, born on the Vardar road
stops.date_confidence: Birth year conventionally 482, with 483 also proposed; the traditional day, 11 May, is not securely attested by anything, and the date here defaults to 01-01. Coordinate corrected: the research pool gave 41.9773 / 21.5644, which falls in the southern outskirts of Skopje, and elsewhere gave 42 / 21.4, which is Skopje itself. Wikipedia 'Taor' puts the archaeological site at 41.898 / 21.611, some 20 km southeast on the left bank of the Vardar.
stops.campa: A son is born to Sabbatius and Vigilantia in a Latin-speaking village of Dardania, twenty miles up the Vardar from Scupi, and they name him Petrus Sabbatius. The province is army country, poor and hard, the sort of place a family exports its sons from. His uncle Justin has already walked out of it toward Constantinople and the palace guard. The boy will rule the Roman world for thirty-eight years and will not see this valley again, though he will pay it back in stone. The eleventh of May rests on nothing that can be checked.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Justinian I', citing Evans, The Age of Justinian
suggested_refs: The Tauresium excavation at Taor, southeast of Skopje
Procopius, Buildings 4.1, on the emperor's native ground

stops.name: Constantinople, the uncle's household
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No ancient source fixes when Justin sent for his nephew, adopted him, or had him educated; the date is a placeholder to order the segment. The research pool tagged this event inconsistently, attested in one lens and reconstruction in another; the reconstruction reading is followed here. Pin inherited from empress_theodora.journey.json for the Great Palace.
stops.campa: Justin sends for his sister's son. No source says when, and none says what the boy carried on the road. He arrives in the capital, is adopted, takes the name Iustinianus from his uncle, and is educated as men are educated who are meant for the palace: law, theology, Latin kept and Greek acquired. Justin meanwhile is climbing inside the Excubitors, the emperor's own guard, and a family of Dardanian peasants now has two men in the palace. What the younger one did in those years, and in what office if any, is not recorded anywhere.
sources: Procopius, Secret History, on the family's origins
suggested_refs: The Excubitors, the palace guard regiment through which the family rose

stops.name: The Hippodrome, the Excubitors raise Justin
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day for Justin's accession (Wikipedia, 'Justin I'). The tradition that the guard first offered the purple to Justinian and that he declined it in his uncle's favour is late, comes from Byzantine chroniclers, and is read by modern historians as retrojection; it is carried here as tradition only. Hippodrome pin inherited from empress_theodora.journey.json.
stops.campa: Anastasius dies without an heir and the palace factions spend a night failing to agree. In the morning the guard settles it: Justin, commander of the Excubitors, past sixty and said by his enemies to be illiterate, is acclaimed emperor. Justinian is about thirty-six, and no source of the time gives him an office. A later tradition says the guard offered the purple first to the nephew, who refused it in his uncle's favour. The chroniclers who report that are writing in the following centuries, with the ending already in their hands.
sources: Later Byzantine chronicle tradition on the offered purple, as summarized in the research pool
suggested_refs: The kathisma of the Hippodrome, where emperors were shown to the city

stops.name: The Great Palace, the schism closed and the army given
stops.date_confidence: Year attested for the offices; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. The end of the Acacian Schism is dated 519, the murder of Vitalian and the field command 520. Justinian's own part in the killing is disputed in the sources and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Within a year of his uncle's accession he has done the thing Anastasius would never do: sent to Rome, accepted the pope's terms, and ended the thirty-five-year Acacian schism that had split the churches of the two capitals. Then the general Vitalian, who had once besieged Constantinople and was now consul, is murdered at a palace banquet, and what Justinian's hand was in it the sources do not agree about. He takes the field command in the capital, the rank of patrician, the title nobilissimus.
sources: Britannica-derived chronology of the reign of Justin I
suggested_refs: The formula of Pope Hormisdas, signed at Constantinople in 519

segments.name: The Purple Assumed, and the Law Given Once

stops.name: The Hippodrome, the consul's games
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; the consular year opened 1 January, which is also the default here. Marcellinus Comes, Chronicle s.a. 521, is the near-contemporary notice of the expenditure.
stops.campa: He holds the ordinary consulship and spends on the inaugural games at a rate the city has not seen in living memory: beasts by the hundred in the arena, distributions to the crowd, the whole apparatus of a man buying a public. The consulship is a hollow office by now, an expensive year of ceremony with no power attached to it, and that is exactly why the spending reads as an argument rather than a party. Justin has no son. The nephew is showing the Hippodrome what the succession is going to look like.
suggested_refs: The consular diptychs of the 520s, the surviving material of these games

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, the actress married
stops.date_confidence: Year given as 525 by the research pool; the atlas's own empress_theodora.journey.json dates the marriage c. 524-525 and stages it in the old Constantinian church on this site. The two are not reconciled here and the range is stated. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. Pin inherited byte-identically from the sibling file.
stops.campa: He marries Theodora, daughter of a Hippodrome bear-keeper, an actress off the stage and back from the Pentapolis and Alexandria, in the old Constantinian church that stands where his own will stand. Roman law forbade a senator to marry a woman of the theatre; Justin's constitution lifted the bar for repentant actresses, which is to say for one woman. The empress Euphemia had objected while she lived and is now dead. He is past forty. In the seventeen years he outlives Theodora he will not marry again.
suggested_refs: Codex Justinianus 5.4.23, the law written for one marriage
The atlas file for Empress Theodora, which carries the pre-marriage biography

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, crowned in his uncle's lifetime
stops.date_confidence: Day attested, but tagged differently by the research pool's own two lenses: reconstruction in the chronology lens after Wikipedia 'Justin I', attested in the geography lens after Chronicon Paschale s.a. 527. The disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Justin is dying, of an old wound in the foot that has turned. On the first of April he raises his nephew to Augustus, and the two of them are crowned together, Justinian and Theodora, in the church where they were married. The Roman world now has two emperors and one of them cannot walk. For four months the arrangement holds, and the business of the empire moves entirely through the younger man's hands. Whether the old emperor decided this or was shown a decision already taken, the chroniclers do not agree and cannot be made to.
suggested_refs: The old Constantinian Hagia Sophia, burned five years later in the Nika riots

stops.name: The Great Palace, sole emperor
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day (Wikipedia, 'Justin I').
stops.campa: Justin dies on the first of August and the peasant's nephew from Tauresium is sole ruler of the Roman empire, forty-five years old, with a wife the aristocracy will never forgive him for and a programme already drafted. He has watched Anastasius govern and he has watched his uncle govern, and he holds a view of the office that neither of them held: that the emperor is the source of the law, of the doctrine and of the order, and that the three are one job. He will hold it for thirty-eight years.
suggested_refs: The Novels of Justinian, in which the theory of the office is stated in his own voice

stops.name: The Great Palace, the first Codex
stops.date_confidence: Promulgation attested to the day by the constitution Summa rei publicae. Correction carried: the research pool's geography lens says the Codex 'takes effect' on 7 April, conflating promulgation with entry into force. It was promulgated 7 April and in force from 16 April 529.
stops.campa: Seven months into the reign he appoints ten men, John of Cappadocia at their head, to gather every imperial constitution still in force since Hadrian and throw the rest away. Two years later the constitution Summa rei publicae promulgates the result and gives it force from the sixteenth of April. Law that had contradicted itself across a thousand rolls is one book now, and nothing outside the book is law. Of this first edition only fragments survive. A revised Codex replaces it in 534.
suggested_refs: The constitution Summa rei publicae, 7 April 529
The Codex Iustinianus repetitae praelectionis of 534, which replaced this edition

stops.name: Athens, the last teachers
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The teaching law is dated 529 and organized philosophical instruction under Damascius ends about then, but the causal link is disputed by modern historians and John Malalas, Chronicle 18.47, is a hostile and compressed witness. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The phrase 'Justinian closed the Academy' overstates a continuous institution that had not existed for centuries.
stops.campa: A law of the same year forbids the unbaptized to teach. In Athens the philosophical school that traced its descent from Plato, in this generation under Damascius, stops; its last teachers go east to the Persian court and come back disappointed. The endowments are seized. The emperor never sets foot in the city, and Malalas, who reports the law, is a hostile witness writing compressed notices decades afterward. Whether the law closed the school or found it already dying is argued still.
sources: Codex Justinianus I.11.10.2 (529), as cited in the atlas file for Plato
suggested_refs: Codex Justinianus I.11.10.2, the instrument cited for the end of the Athenian succession
Agathias, Histories 2.30-31, on the philosophers at Khosrow's court

stops.name: The Great Palace, the Digest closed against commentary
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: Digest promulgated 16 December 533, in force 30 December. The Institutes were promulgated 21 November 533 with the same effective date, and the second Codex on 16 November 534, in force 29 December; both are folded into this stop rather than given their own. The commission was ordered by Deo auctore, 15 December 530.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of December 530 the constitution Deo auctore had put Tribonian at the head of a second commission with a harder job: read the whole classical jurisprudence, three million lines of Ulpian and Paul and Papinian, and cut it to a fiftieth. Three years later the Digest is promulgated with the force of statute, and commentary on it is forbidden, so that no jurist can start the confusion over again. The Institutes for students came out a month earlier. A revised Codex follows in 534.
sources: Constitutio Tanta and Dedoken, prefaces to the Digest
suggested_refs: The Littera Florentina, the sixth-century Digest manuscript through which the text survived
The recovery and teaching of the Digest in northern Italy from about 1070, seed of the medieval law schools

segments.name: Dara, Callinicum, and the Cry of Nika

stops.name: Dara, the fortress against Persia
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day not fixed, defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected: the research pool gave 40.9761, which falls in open country east of the ruins. Wikipedia 'Dara (Mesopotamia)' gives 37.1778 / 40.9411 and 'Battle of Dara' gives 37.18 / 40.955. The site is at Oguz in Mardin province, Turkey, not on the Syrian border strip as the pool's chronology lens loosely states.
stops.campa: The fortress Anastasius built against Persia, ten miles from Nisibis, and the emperor has been strengthening it since the day he came to the throne. Belisarius, in his first independent command, digs a ditch in front of an outnumbered line and breaks a Sasanian army against it. It is the first return on the frontier money, and the emperor is a thousand miles away, reading the dispatch. On the staff at Dara is a young legal adviser out of Caesarea named Procopius, taking notes.
suggested_refs: The cisterns and walls of Dara at Oguz, Mardin province

stops.name: Callinicum, the Euphrates bank
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Correction carried: the pool's geography lens calls this 'Belisarius's outnumbered force', contradicting its own chronology lens. Wikipedia 'Battle of Callinicum' gives Roman and allied strength 20,000-25,000 against Sasanian 15,000-20,000. The Endless Peace of 532 is folded into this stop; the pool sited its conclusion in the Chrysotriklinos, a hall built a generation later under Justin II, and that room name is dropped.
stops.campa: A year later the same general meets Azarethes on the Euphrates bank on Easter Saturday with the larger army, and handles it badly. The Roman line breaks and holds only because the infantry backs to the river and stands there until dark; both sides are too cut up to campaign again that season, and a commission of enquiry is sent out from the capital to establish whose fault it was. Then Kavadh dies, and his son Khosrow sells Justinian a peace with no end date on it for eleven thousand pounds of gold. He pays.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.22, on the Endless Peace
suggested_refs: The terms of the Endless Peace of 532, broken by Khosrow eight years later

stops.name: The Hippodrome, the factions cry Nika
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. The death toll of roughly 30,000 given by Procopius and repeated since is not independently verifiable and is treated here as a source's figure, not a fact. Hippodrome pin inherited from empress_theodora.journey.json.
stops.campa: Blue and Green have been rioting over the execution of two of their own, and at the races on the thirteenth the factions do the one thing they never do, which is agree. The cry in the stands turns from the name of a horse to Nika, conquer, and the crowd goes out through the gates toward the palace. By the fifth day the senate house is burning, the Constantinian Hagia Sophia is burning, and Hypatius, nephew of Anastasius and unwilling, has been carried to the kathisma and crowned with a chain of somebody's gold.
suggested_refs: The burnt layer under the Augustaion, archaeological trace of the January fires

stops.name: The Great Palace, the ships at the steps
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the scene and the words. The council is plausible and the outcome is attested; the speech is Procopius's composition in the ancient manner, not a transcript, and the words quoted are Theodora's, not Justinian's. The common English form 'the purple makes a fine winding-sheet' is a paraphrase from secondary literature, not this translation. Day placed inside the riot week, which ran 13-18 January.
stops.campa: Ships are ready at the harbour steps and the emperor's council is discussing which of them to take. The empress speaks against it. Procopius gives her a speech and the speech is his own writing, but the council is real and so is what follows, which is that nobody boards. Belisarius, Mundus and the eunuch Narses go out instead, Narses carrying gold to split the Blues off from the Greens and the other two carrying soldiers. Justinian is fifty and has been sole emperor for four and a half years.
stops.quote: For as for myself, I approve a certain ancient saying that royalty is a good burial-shroud
stops.quote_source: Theodora, as composed by Procopius, Wars 1.24, trans. H. B. Dewing, Loeb Classical Library 1914, via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The harbour of Boukoleon and the palace steps, where the ships were waiting

stops.name: The Hippodrome, the reckoning on the sand
stops.date_confidence: The suppression is dated to 18 January and the executions of Hypatius and Pompeius to the day after, without formal trial. The confiscated property was partly restored to their families later. The casualty figure is Procopius's and is not independently attested.
stops.campa: The two commanders come in from opposite ends of the Hippodrome with the crowd penned between them and the exits held, and they kill until there is nothing standing. Procopius says thirty thousand; nobody can check the figure and everybody repeats it. Hypatius and his brother Pompeius are executed the next day without trial and their estates taken, part of it handed back to their sons years later. He has his city back. The quarter between the palace and the burnt church is ash all the way to the Augustaion.
suggested_refs: The confiscation and partial restitution of the estates of Hypatius and Pompeius

segments.name: The Great Church and the Building Programme

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, the first stone on the burnt ground
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. The words quoted are given by Procopius as Justinian's own speech to the architects, the only place in Buildings 1.1 where the emperor is quoted directly rather than described.
stops.campa: Forty days after the fires he begins again on the same ground, and not with an architect: with Anthemius of Tralles, who writes on conic sections and burning mirrors, and Isidore of Miletus, who edits Archimedes. What they are asked for has no precedent, a dome on pendentives over a square, and the great eastern arch starts to fail while it is going up. The masons stop work and refuse to close it. The emperor tells them to close it anyway, and Procopius, who despised him in another book, records the reasoning.
stops.quote: For when it rests upon itself, it will no longer need the props beneath it
stops.quote_source: Justinian to the architects Anthemius and Isidorus, in Procopius, Buildings 1.1.71, trans. H. B. Dewing, Loeb Classical Library 1940, via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Anthemius of Tralles, On Remarkable Mechanical Devices
Rowland Mainstone, Hagia Sophia: Architecture, Structure and Liturgy

stops.name: Justiniana Prima, the city raised on his own ground
stops.date_confidence: Foundation dated 535 by Novel 11, which erects the see; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. The identification of Caricin Grad near Lebane with Justiniana Prima is the standard one but rests on archaeology and Procopius together, not on an inscription naming the city.
stops.campa: He builds a city where he came from, or near enough: walls, an aqueduct, baths, a cathedral, on a spur above the plain in the country he left as a boy. Novel 11 makes it an archbishopric answering to no metropolitan, which lifts the church of his birthplace clear of every existing hierarchy in the Balkans. It works as an administrative capital for about a century and then it is nothing, abandoned to the Slavs, its street grid readable now only from the air. He never came back to look at it.
suggested_refs: The excavated street grid and episcopal basilica at Caricin Grad, near Lebane

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, the dedication
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day; five years and ten months from the first stone. The exclamation about Solomon is a later reported tradition, unattested at the ceremony by any contemporary source, and neither the geography nor the afterlife lens of the research pool could locate a primary origin for it. Carried here as tradition, in the register, and marked as such.
stops.campa: Five years and ten months from the first stone, tens of thousands of workmen and the revenue of a province later, the emperor and the patriarch Menas dedicate the church. A tradition reported late, by nobody who was standing there, has him walk in and say: Solomon, I have surpassed you. What is not in doubt is the building. It is the largest interior anyone has raised, and the dome sits so lightly on its ring of windows that the sixth century cannot account for it and says instead that the thing hangs from heaven on a chain.
suggested_refs: Paul the Silentiary, Ekphrasis of Hagia Sophia
Later travellers' descriptions of the interior, from Rabban Bar Sauma in the 1280s to Le Corbusier's notebooks

stops.name: Sinai, the walls round the bush
stops.date_confidence: The fortification is dated to the period 548-565 and cannot be fixed more closely; month and day defaulted to 01-01. Pin inherited byte-identically from the atlas files for Catherine of Alexandria, Egeria and Anthony the Great, all of which carry the same Justinianic attribution from Procopius.
stops.campa: At the foot of the mountain where Moses is said to have seen the bush, a settlement of hermits has been living around a chapel attributed to Helena and losing men to raiders. The emperor sends engineers and a garrison and encloses the whole site in granite, a fortress with a church inside it, at the far end of Egypt from anything he governs directly. Procopius lists the work in the Buildings among the ordinary provincial items, a wall and a garrison and a church, costed like the rest. Monks are living inside those walls today.
suggested_refs: Egeria's account of the same site in the 380s, when the walls were still a hundred and seventy years off

stops.name: Nicomedia, the shrine of Pantaleon rebuilt
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Procopius in the Buildings, composed about 554 to 560; the year here is a placeholder inside the building programme and cannot be fixed more closely. Pin and placeholder date inherited byte-identically from saint_pantaleon.journey.json, which also carries the correction that the testimony points at Nicomedia and not at Constantinople.
stops.campa: Procopius, writing the Buildings to the emperor's credit, records in a single sentence that he rebuilt the shrine of Pantaleon at Nicomedia. The physician was killed in that city under Diocletian, two and a half centuries earlier, and buried by Christians in a grave whose location no surviving source describes. Imperial money is now paying for a roof over it, which means somebody in Nicomedia still knew where the grave was. No published list of his principal works includes the item.
sources: Procopius, De aedificiis, on the Nicomedia shrine
suggested_refs: The atlas file for Saint Pantaleon, which carries the cult and the relics

stops.name: Ad Decimum, the tenth milestone
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day for Ad Decimum, 13 September 533; the entry into Carthage two days later, 15 September, is folded into this stop rather than given its own.
stops.campa: Gelimer has deposed the pro-Roman Hilderic, and the emperor has his pretext. Belisarius sails with some fifteen thousand men and lands unopposed; at the tenth milestone south of Carthage the Vandal plan miscarries in three directions at once, Gelimer's brother Ammatas is killed, and the road opens. Two days later the general walks into Carthage without a fight and eats the dinner cooked in the palace kitchen for the king, at the king's table, off the king's plate. A hundred years of Vandal Africa ends inside one week of September.
suggested_refs: The Byrsa hill and the Vandal royal palace at Carthage

stops.name: Tricamarum, the last Vandal army
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Coordinate corrected: the research pool gave 36.7833 / 10.0333, which sits south of the Medjerda, whose course at that longitude runs near 36.85-36.90. The battle was fought about 150 stades, roughly 27 km, west of Carthage on the river's banks.
stops.campa: Gelimer comes back in December with his brother Tzazon and the army recalled from Sardinia, and loses it all in an afternoon on the Medjerda west of Carthage. Tzazon is killed. The king runs to a Berber village in the Numidian hills and holds out through the winter on siege rations before surrendering in the spring. The kingdom that sacked Rome in 455 is a province again, and the emperor who has never seen the country takes the titles Vandalicus and Africanus.
suggested_refs: The praetorian prefecture of Africa, erected over the conquered kingdom in 534

stops.name: The Hippodrome, Gelimer walked through the city
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; the triumph is placed before the end of 534 and the month is not fixed, so the date defaults to 01-01. Correction carried: the research pool's chronology lens makes Belisarius consul in 534. He held the ordinary consulship for 535, entering office on 1 January 535, after the triumph. The two honours are a year apart.
stops.campa: Belisarius is given the ancient consular triumph and walks it on foot from his house to the Hippodrome: the Vandal treasure carried past, Gelimer in the procession saying vanity of vanities, and among the plate the vessels Titus took from the Temple of Solomon in the year seventy and the Vandals took from Rome in four fifty-five. The emperor and empress sit in the kathisma, and the general does obeisance in front of them, which no triumphing Roman had ever done. The consulship follows the next January.
suggested_refs: The consular fasti for 535, giving Belisarius as consul ordinarius

stops.name: Jerusalem, the vessels sent on
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The episode rests on a single passage of Procopius, Wars 4.9, which the research pool could not fetch directly in this pass; nothing further is recorded of the vessels anywhere. Date follows the triumph and is a placeholder. Temple Mount pin inherited byte-identically from aaron_the_levite.journey.json.
stops.campa: Procopius says a Jewish onlooker in Constantinople warned that the Temple plate had ruined every palace that housed it, from Rome to Carthage, and that the emperor took the warning seriously enough to send the vessels on to the Christian churches of Jerusalem. It is the only order of his reign that reaches the Temple Mount, given by a man who never travelled south of the Bosphorus. The whole record for it is one paragraph in one hostile author. Nothing further is heard of the vessels, in Jerusalem or anywhere else.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.9, not fetched directly in this pass
suggested_refs: The Temple furnishings as the atlas carries them in the files for Solomon and Aaron the Levite

stops.name: Naples, in through the aqueduct
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; the siege ran in the autumn of 536 but the day of the entry is not fixed in the sources used, so the date defaults to 01-01.
stops.campa: Sicily has fallen in a single season and the mainland is next. Naples shuts its gates on Belisarius and holds them for three weeks. The sack, when it comes, runs further than the general intended, and it teaches every town between there and Rome what refusing an imperial army will cost; the towns north of it open their gates without a siege. The way in was the old aqueduct. A soldier finds the channel running under the wall unguarded, and four hundred men go through it in the dark and open the city from inside.
suggested_refs: The Bolla aqueduct channel at Naples, the way in

stops.name: Rome, the Porta Asinaria
stops.date_confidence: Entry attested to the day, 9 December 536. The siege under Witigis, which ran from March 537 for a year and nine days along the Aurelian walls, is folded into this stop. The Asinaria pin is used for both this entry and the loss of the city in 546, so that one gate carries one coordinate.
stops.campa: The Gothic garrison marches out of the Flaminian gate as Belisarius comes in at the Asinaria, and Rome changes hands in December without a blow struck. Then Witigis brings up an army the Roman sources put in six figures, and the recovery becomes a siege: the aqueducts cut, mills turned by boats moored in the Tiber, the mausoleum of Hadrian defended by breaking the statues off it and throwing them down on the men at the foot of the wall, the population starving inside its own walls for a year and nine days. The city holds.
suggested_refs: The Aurelian walls and the Castel Sant'Angelo, held through the siege of 537-538

stops.name: Ravenna, the crown he did not take
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; the surrender of Ravenna falls in May 540 but the day is not fixed in the sources used, so the date defaults to 01-01. Whether Justinian read the stratagem as loyalty or as a threat is not settled by any source and is left open here. Milan, destroyed in 539 with a casualty figure Procopius gives as 300,000 adult males and which is not credible as arithmetic, is not given a stop.
stops.campa: The Goths, beaten back into their capital, offer to make Belisarius emperor of the West if he will take it. He lets them believe he will, walks into Ravenna, and takes king, treasury and kingdom in his own emperor's name instead. Then he sails home with Witigis and the Gothic gold, and no triumph is voted him this time, as one was voted for Africa six years before. Whether Justinian read the manoeuvre as loyalty, or as a demonstration of what his general could have had for the asking, is nowhere recorded.
suggested_refs: The Gothic royal palace at Ravenna, taken intact in 540

stops.name: Antioch, the city carried into Persia
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; the sack falls in the campaigning season of 540 and the day is not fixed in the sources used, so the date defaults to 01-01.
stops.campa: Khosrow reads the western victories correctly, declares the endless peace ended, and comes down the Euphrates. Antioch, third city of the empire, is stormed and burned, and the survivors are marched into Mesopotamia and settled in a new town outside Ctesiphon that the shah names Khosrow's Better Antioch, laid out street for street on the city he has just burned. The emperor has an army in Italy, an army in Africa and no reserve anywhere. The eleven thousand pounds of gold bought six years.
suggested_refs: Weh Antiok Khosrow, the deportees' city built near Ctesiphon

stops.name: The Great Palace, the fall of John the Cappadocian
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Procopius is the only detailed source and is hostile in both the Wars and the Secret History, so the mechanics of the trap need caution even where the prosecution itself is documented. The lapse of the annual consulship is dated to the same year.
stops.campa: The praetorian prefect has raised the money for all of it, the wars and the buildings and the law, by methods that made him the most hated man in the empire and the most useful man in it. Antonina and the empress lay a trap baited with a fabricated conspiracy and he walks into it: stripped of office and rank, ordained a priest against his will, sent to Egypt. The revenue never recovers its efficiency. In the same year the emperor lets the annual consulship lapse, and after nine hundred years Rome stops naming consuls.
sources: Research pool synthesis on the fasti consulares
suggested_refs: The fasti consulares, which end as an annual series in 541

stops.name: Constantinople, the pits above the harbour
stops.date_confidence: The plague reaches the capital in 541-542; the emperor's own illness and recovery fall in 542 and are folded into this stop. Month and day not fixed, defaulted to 01-01. Ancient DNA from graves of the period has identified Yersinia pestis; total mortality is disputed and no figure is stated here as fact.
stops.campa: Plague comes up from Egypt in the grain ships. The dead outrun the graves, then the cemeteries, then the burial crews; bodies go into the towers of the Sycae fortifications and into pits above the Golden Horn until the wind carries the city's smell out to the shipping. The emperor catches it and does not die. While he lies swollen and senseless the generals in the east discuss the succession out loud, and the empress has that conversation reported to her, and arrests Buzes for it when he comes back.
suggested_refs: Ancient-DNA identification of Yersinia pestis in sixth-century graves

stops.name: Rome, the Porta Asinaria opened from inside
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Correction carried: the research pool's geography lens places this at the Salarian Gate with coordinates 41.9145 / 12.5044, which is about a kilometre from the Salaria site and three from where the event happened. Wikipedia 'Sack of Rome (546)' has the Goths entering by the Porta Asinaria, opened by Isaurian defectors who scaled the wall at night.
stops.campa: Totila has taken back nearly everything, and Belisarius, sent to Italy with too few men and no money at all, cannot hold the city he saved nine years earlier. Isaurian deserters go over the wall in the night and open the Asinaria from inside, the same gate the Romans came in at. Justinian is fighting Persia and plague at the same time, and Italy gets whatever is left over, which in this year is nothing. The city will change hands twice more before the war ends. Totila empties it of inhabitants, and for forty days nobody lives in Rome at all.
suggested_refs: The Porta Asinaria in the Aurelian walls, entered in 536 and again in 546

stops.name: San Vitale, the panel he never saw
stops.date_confidence: Consecration dated 547; month and day not fixed, defaulted to 01-01. Justinian probably never visited Ravenna in person and certainly did not attend. Pin inherited byte-identically from empress_theodora.journey.json.
stops.campa: An octagonal church in Ravenna is consecrated, and on the sanctuary wall, in glass and gold, the emperor stands crowned and haloed with a paten in his hands, Bishop Maximian beside him and guards behind, facing Theodora with her chalice across the apse. Ravenna has been imperial again for seven years and the war for the rest of Italy has another seven to run. The panels say who owns the recovered West, and they say it in glass, to Italians, at the altar end where only the clergy stand. Maximian's name is set in letters above his own head. Neither of the two ever entered the building.
sources: Agnellus of Ravenna, Liber Pontificalis Ecclesiae Ravennatis
suggested_refs: The apse mosaics of San Vitale, visited and written about by later travellers from Charlemagne's agents to Yeats, Klimt, Hesse, Mackintosh, Rivera and Sarah Bernhardt

stops.name: The Great Palace, the death of Theodora
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Correction carried: the research pool's geography lens stages the death at the mausoleum of the Holy Apostles, conflating death with burial, and gives a coordinate that disagrees with its own afterlife lens and with empress_theodora.journey.json. She died in the Great Palace and was buried at the Holy Apostles in porphyry. Both pins are taken from the sibling file.
stops.campa: Theodora dies in the palace after a long illness, about forty-eight, twenty-three years married, and is carried to the mausoleum at the Holy Apostles and laid in porphyry. The anti-Chalcedonian clergy she sheltered in the palace of Hormisdas stay exactly where she put them. Procopius, who hated them both, is the only witness to the marriage from inside, and he is not a witness anyone can rely on. Justinian rules seventeen more years, appoints nobody in her place, and goes on naming her in his legislation and in the oaths he requires.
suggested_refs: The porphyry sarcophagus of Theodora in the Holy Apostles mausoleum
The atlas file for Empress Theodora, which carries her own journey

segments.name: The Three Chapters, and Italy Ended

stops.name: Taginae, Totila's army broken
stops.date_confidence: Dated to July 552; the day is given variously and is not fixed here, so it defaults to 01. Also called Busta Gallorum, near modern Gualdo Tadino.
stops.campa: Narses is seventy-five, a eunuch and a chamberlain, and has been given what Belisarius was never given: money, men, and no colleague. He meets Totila in the Apennines above Gualdo Tadino with archers on both wings and a dismounted centre, and destroys the Gothic army in an afternoon. Totila is speared in the flight and dies before nightfall in a village called Caprae; the bloodied cap and cloak go to Constantinople as evidence. The emperor is seventy and has spent eighteen years on Italy.
suggested_refs: The plain of Busta Gallorum, near Gualdo Tadino

stops.name: Mons Lactarius, the last king
stops.date_confidence: Dated 1 or 30 October 552 depending on the source; defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected: the research pool put this on 'the slopes of Vesuvius' at 40.7614 / 14.4939, which is the Sarno plain. Mons Lactarius is the Monti Lattari, a separate range above Nocera and Lettere; Teia camped first at the foot of Vesuvius and then withdrew into the hills.
stops.campa: Teia, the last king the Goths elect, comes south to relieve Cumae and is cornered in the Lattari hills above Nocera, the range that looks across at Vesuvius from the other side of the plain. Two months of blockade, then a fight the sources describe as an infantry match on a slope. The survivors are allowed to leave Italy under oath, and organized Gothic power in the peninsula ends there, on ground used for grazing goats. Teia goes down in the front rank, holding a shield stuck so full of spears that he has to keep calling for another one.
suggested_refs: The Monti Lattari above Lettere and Nocera

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, the Second Council
stops.date_confidence: Council sessions attested, 5 May to 2 June 553. Pope Vigilius's detention in and around the Palace of Hormisdas from 547 to 555, including the violence at the altar he was clinging to, is reconstruction from the Liber Pontificalis and Victor of Tunnuna and is folded into this stop rather than given its own.
stops.campa: Pope Vigilius has been in the city since 547, brought from Rome under imperial pressure, dragged off an altar he was holding on to, changing his position on the Three Chapters four times under threat. The council meets without him for four weeks and condemns the writings, which is what the emperor wants in order to bring the eastern Miaphysites back inside Chalcedon. The Miaphysites are not reconciled. Northern Italy goes into schism over it for a hundred and fifty years. Vigilius signs afterward and dies on the road home.
sources: Acts of the Second Council of Constantinople
suggested_refs: The Palace of Hormisdas, refuge and place of detention of Pope Vigilius
The Istrian schism, which outlasted every party to the quarrel

stops.name: The Great Palace, the Pragmatic Sanction
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Correction carried twice: the research pool sites the constitution at Ravenna under 'exarchal administration'. It was issued at Constantinople, addressed to Narses and the prefect Antiochus, and the Exarchate of Ravenna is first attested only around 584, thirty years later; Italy from 554 was governed as a praetorian prefecture. The pool also dates the Frankish and Alamannic defeat at the Volturnus to 552 in one lens and 554 in another; 554 is correct.
stops.campa: He issues from Constantinople, to Narses and the prefect Antiochus, the constitution that reorganizes what is left of Italy: senatorial property restored where it can be traced, selected acts of the Gothic kings confirmed, Totila's grants voided, the peninsula folded into the empire as a prefecture. In the autumn Narses breaks a Frankish and Alamannic invasion at the Volturnus near Capua. Rome has changed hands five times, Milan is gone, the aqueducts are cut and the senate is finished. Italy is a praetorian prefecture again, run out of Constantinople through Narses, who will govern it for the next thirteen years.
sources: Pragmatic Sanction pro petitione Vigilii, Novellae Appendix VII
suggested_refs: The praetorian prefecture of Italy, 554-584, before any exarch existed

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, the east end comes down
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Correction carried: both lenses of the research pool say 'the first dome collapsed'. Wikipedia 'Hagia Sophia' has the 553 and 557 quakes cracking the main dome and eastern semi-dome, and on 7 May 558 the eastern portion falling into the sanctuary and destroying the ambon, altar and ciborium. The rebuilding and the second dedication of 24 December 562 are folded into this stop.
stops.campa: Earthquakes in 553 and again in December 557 crack the main dome and the eastern semi-dome. On the seventh of May the east end comes down into the sanctuary and takes the ambon, the altar and the ciborium with it. He is seventy-six, and he rebuilds. Isidore the Younger, nephew of the first Isidore, raises the dome some twenty feet higher and lighter than his uncle's, and on Christmas Eve 562 the church is dedicated a second time, with Paul the Silentiary reciting a long poem about the lamps.
sources: Paul the Silentiary, Ekphrasis of Hagia Sophia
suggested_refs: Paul the Silentiary's Ekphrasis, recited at the rededication of 562

stops.name: Melantias, the old general called out again
stops.date_confidence: Dated to March 559; the day is not fixed and defaults to 01. Coordinate corrected: the research pool gave 41.045 / 28.585, roughly 33 km west of Hagia Sophia out toward Silivri. Wikipedia 'Battle of Melantias' places Melantias about 20 km west of the city, conventionally near modern Yarimburgaz. Justinian's own ride into Thrace after the raid is folded into this stop; Agathias shows him working diplomacy, and no source shows him in a pitched battle at any point in his life.
stops.campa: Zabergan's Kutrigurs cross the Danube on the ice, come through frontier works the earthquakes have broken, and reach twenty kilometres from the walls. There is no field army in Thrace. The emperor calls Belisarius out of retirement; the old general scrapes together three hundred veterans, some guards and a crowd of farmers, and stops the raid with an ambush in wooded ground. Then Justinian rides out into Thrace himself, the only journey of his reign beyond the capital's neighbourhood, and finishes the business by paying the Utigurs to attack the Kutrigurs.
suggested_refs: The Long Walls of Thrace, breached by the raid of 559

stops.name: The Great Palace, fifty years bought, and a conspiracy
stops.date_confidence: Year attested for both the treaty and the conspiracy; months not fixed, defaulted to 01-01. The research pool flags that it did not re-verify the conspiracy against a primary text in this pass; it comes through Malalas 18.129 in the Tusculan fragment and Theophanes. The medieval legend of a blinded, begging Belisarius has no ancient support at all.
stops.campa: He and Khosrow sign a fifty-year peace: Lazica stays Roman, and Rome pays an annual sum described in the treaty as a contribution to the defence of the Caucasus passes rather than as tribute. In the same year bankers are arrested over a plot against the emperor and name Belisarius under interrogation. The picture of that general blind at a gate with a begging bowl is a medieval invention with no source older than the Middle Ages. What happens is that he loses his honours, is confined to his own house, and is restored the following July.
suggested_refs: Menander Protector's account of the fifty-year treaty terms

stops.name: The Great Palace, the incorruptible body
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The edict does not survive; there is no text to examine, and this is an absence in the record rather than a failure of access. Everything known comes from Evagrius Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History 4.39, writing later. Dated January 565 by convention and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: In his last winter the emperor is reported to have issued an edict requiring the bishops to hold that Christ's body was incorruptible from the moment of the Incarnation, which no council had taught and which the Chalcedonians regarded as heresy coming at them from the other side. The document does not survive; everything anyone knows of it comes through Evagrius, writing afterward, with nothing to check him against. Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, refuses to subscribe, and is deposed and sent into exile. The emperor is eighty-two.
suggested_refs: The deposition of Patriarch Eutychius, January 565, and his restoration in 577

stops.name: The Great Palace, the night of the thirteenth
stops.date_confidence: Attested: he died in the night of 13 to 14 November 565, apparently of natural causes. The succession claim is reconstruction: Callinicus's report that the dying emperor named Justin comes through Corippus, In laudem Iustini minoris, which the research pool did not open in this pass, and no one else was in the room.
stops.campa: He dies in the night of the thirteenth to the fourteenth of November, about eighty-three, having outlived Theodora by seventeen years, Belisarius by eight months, and Tribonian and Procopius by longer than that. There is no settled successor. Before dawn the chamberlain Callinicus goes to his sister's son Justin and reports that the dying man named him, and Justin reaches the palace with the Excubitors behind him, which is how the first Justin had done it. Whether the naming happened, nobody else was in the room to say.
sources: Corippus, In laudem Iustini minoris 1, not fetched directly in this pass
suggested_refs: Corippus, In laudem Iustini minoris, the panegyric that is the source for the deathbed designation

stops.name: The Church of the Holy Apostles, the mausoleum
stops.date_confidence: Burial in the mausoleum on the north arm, consecrated 28 June 550, is attested; the exact day of the funeral is not fixed and is placed the day after the death. The mausoleum's footprint has never been archaeologically fixed and lies under the Fatih Mosque complex. Pin inherited byte-identically from empress_theodora.journey.json. The later events in this campa are the site's own history, not stops.
stops.campa: He is buried beside Theodora in the mausoleum on the north arm of the Church of the Holy Apostles, in the row of Christian emperors that begins with Constantine. Crusaders break the imperial tombs open for gold and gems in 1204. The Ottomans pull the ruined church down in 1461 and put the Fatih Mosque on the ground. The bronze horseman he set over the Augustaion loses the orb from its hand between 1422 and 1427, falls in the earthquake of 1509, and is melted down for cannon. Hagia Sophia is still standing.
sources: Nicetas Choniates, on the sack of 1204
suggested_refs: The Column of Justinian in the Augustaion, raised 543, fallen 1509
The Fatih Mosque complex, built over the site of the imperial mausoleum
